problem: Prior pursuit-evasion work mostly targets capturing an evader and relies on offline environment decomposition (information graphs, Voronoi) whose cost scales with map size. It does not consider maximizing tracking time under a limited-FOV depth sensor, nor an evader that knows the pursuer's visibility region.
motivation: Capture does not guarantee the evader was tracked for the maximal time, yet applications such as discreet patrolling, shadowing and following need persistent visual tracking. The paper therefore frames the task as active tracking in a mapped environment with both a smart pursuer and an adversarial smart evader.
key_idea: A hybrid pursuer combines a reactive visual servo (when the evader is visible) with particle-filter estimation of the evader's map position (when it is not) and navigates to that estimate, against an evader that picks escape points outside the pursuer's ray-cast visibility region.
insight: The smart pursuer clearly beats a random pursuer in all three environments, for example 84.78% vs 17.56% in Complex Hall at speed ratio 2. A smart evader lowers tracking success and increases its variance, so an adversary with access to the pursuer's visibility region is much harder. The smart pursuer still stays at roughly 47-62%, and at half the evader's speed it keeps a high rate. There is no component-level ablation, so the source of the gains is not separated.
method: Detection and tracking: OpenPose person detection gives a bounding box, then Lucas-Kanade tracking. Depth points inside the box give the evader's map position.

Particle filter localization: Sequential Importance Sampling with a unicycle motion model estimates the evader's map position when it is not visible. Weights inside the visibility region are reduced if the evader was not seen, and the reverse if it was seen. Resampling is triggered when N_eff < 0.8N.

Reactive local planner: when the evader is visible, the pursuer computes the bounding-box offset from the image center for angular velocity, and uses mean box depth for linear velocity to hold a fixed following distance.
Global goal for pursuer: when the evader is lost, the pursuer navigates via move_base to the weighted mean of the particles.

Smart evader: it knows the pursuer's pose and computes the pursuer's visibility region by ray casting. It selects a free-space point outside that region that minimizes cost_escape = (evader distance)/(pursuer distance).
Simulation testbed: Gazebo/ROS with a TurtleBot pursuer and a human-model evader in three environments, at speed ratios 0.5/1/2, for 90 s at 1 Hz.

setting.backbone: OpenPose detector + Lucas-Kanade tracker + SIS particle filter + move_base planner (no learned decision model trained by the authors)
setting.observation: forward-facing RGB-D camera with FOV pi/3, plus a prior occupancy grid map
setting.action_space: goal locations executed by move_base with non-holonomic velocity control (linear/angular velocity)
setting.simulator: Gazebo (ROS) plus a real-world TurtleBot/HoloLens demo
setting.privileged: prior occupancy grid map; the smart evader is given the pursuer's pose and visibility region

numbers_note: The paper is not a standard navigation benchmark; results are mean tracking success rates in a custom Gazebo testbed. Enclosed Room and Brick Room S-S and all R-R columns are also in Table 1 but omitted here. The distributions appear only in boxplot figures.
results: In the custom Gazebo tests, the smart pursuer outperforms the random pursuer in every environment and speed ratio, e.g. 78.47% vs 23.85% at ratio 1 in Complex Hall. The smart evader lowers tracking success, e.g. from 84.78% to 52.65% at ratio 2 in Complex Hall, and raises its variance. The smart pursuer still stays at about 47-62% against the smart evader.
limitations: The pursuer is not adversarially aware; it does not model that the evader is also smart, so no equilibrium is analyzed.

The evaluation is limited to a small simulated testbed (40 runs per configuration, 3 maps) with only random-pursuer baselines and no comparison with existing pursuit-evasion methods. Real-world results are only in a video.
It assumes a known map and a single pursuer, and the smart evader has privileged pursuer information.
